smt-2021-power-01d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-01d.body:
The powers of $10\equiv3$ modulo $7$ are $3,2,6,4,5,1$ and then repeat with period $6$ ($10^6\equiv1$). Since $2021=6\cdot336+5$, $10^{2021}\equiv10^5\equiv5$.

**Answer: 5**

smt-2021-power-02a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-02a.body:
$5\cdot3=15=14+1\equiv1\pmod7$, so $k=3$ (the others $k=0,\dots,6$ give $0,5,3,1,6,4,2$ for $5k\bmod 7$, so $k=3$ is the only one).

**Answer: 3**

smt-2021-power-02b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-02b.body: $k\cdot(5n)=(5k)\cdot n\equiv1\cdot n=n\pmod 7$, using $5k\equiv1$ and that congruences can be multiplied. ∎

smt-2021-power-03a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-03a.body: If $ax\equiv ay$ then $p\mid a(x-y)$. Since $p$ is prime and $p\nmid a$, $p\mid x-y$ (a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors, by unique factorisation). So $x\equiv y$. ∎

smt-2021-power-03b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-03b.body: By part (a) (cancellation), the $p$ numbers $0\cdot a,1\cdot a,\dots,(p-1)a$ are pairwise incongruent mod $p$ (if $ia\equiv ja$ then $i\equiv j$, so $i=j$ for $0\le i,j<p$). So they represent all $p$ residues modulo $p$, in particular the residue $1$: some $b$ has $ab\equiv1$. ∎

smt-2021-power-03c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-03c.body: By cancellation, $a,2a,\dots,(p-1)a$ are pairwise incongruent and none is $\equiv0$, so they are the residues $1,\dots,p-1$ in some order. Comparing products: $(p-1)!\,a^{p-1}\equiv(p-1)!\pmod p$. As $p\nmid(p-1)!$, cancel it: $a^{p-1}\equiv1$. ∎

smt-2021-power-03d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-03d.body: Clearing denominators, $bc+ca+ab=abc$ as integers, hence modulo $p$. Multiply by $a^{-1}b^{-1}c^{-1}$ (inverses exist since $a,b,c\not\equiv0$): $a^{-1}+b^{-1}+c^{-1}\equiv1$. ∎

smt-2021-power-04a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-04a.body: Let $p\ge5$; then $2,3,6$ are invertible mod $p$ and by Fermat $x^{p-2}\equiv x^{-1}$ (since $x\cdot x^{p-2}=x^{p-1}\equiv1$). So $a_{p-2}\equiv2^{-1}+3^{-1}+6^{-1}-1$. Multiplying by $6$: $3+2+1-6=0$, so $6\,a_{p-2}\equiv0$ and, as $p\nmid6$, $a_{p-2}\equiv0\pmod p$. ∎

smt-2021-power-04b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-04b.body: It suffices to show every prime divides some term. For $p\ge5$, $p\mid a_{p-2}$ by the previous part. For $p=2$ and $p=3$: $a_2=4+9+36-1=48$ is divisible by both. Hence any integer greater than $1$ has a prime factor that divides some $a_n$, so is not coprime to all terms. Only $1$ remains (and $1$ is coprime to everything). ∎

smt-2021-power-05b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-05b.body:
The elements $a$ and $-a$ are different (else $2a\equiv0$, so $a\equiv0$ as $p$ is odd), and likewise $a^{-1}\ne-a^{-1}$. So the set has fewer than $4$ elements iff $a\equiv a^{-1}$ or $a\equiv-a^{-1}$ (the other coincidences are equivalent to these). $a\equiv a^{-1}$ iff $a^2\equiv1$ iff $a\equiv\pm1$ (as $p\mid(a-1)(a+1)$). $a\equiv-a^{-1}$ iff $a^2\equiv-1$. In these cases the set has exactly $2$ elements: $\{1,-1\}$ or $\{a,-a\}$.

**Answer: $a\equiv\pm1$, or $a^2\equiv-1\pmod p$.**

smt-2021-power-05c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-05c.body: Suppose $a$ is a solution. Then $-a$ is also a solution, and $-a\not\equiv a$ since otherwise $2a\equiv0$, so $a\equiv0$, but then $a^2+1\equiv1\ne0$. If $b$ is any solution then $p\mid a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)$, so $b\equiv\pm a$. Hence the solutions are exactly $\pm a$: two of them. So the number of solutions is $0$ or $2$. ∎

smt-2021-power-05d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-05d.body: The classes $\{a,-a,a^{-1},-a^{-1}\}$ partition $\{1,\dots,p-1\}$ (they are the orbits of a group of four maps acting on the nonzero residues). By part (b) the class of $1$ is $\{1,-1\}$ of size $2$, the classes of solutions of $a^2\equiv-1$ have size $2$ (and, by (c), there is exactly one such class if a solution exists, none otherwise), and all others have size $4$. Hence $p-1\equiv2\pmod4$ if there is no solution, and $p-1\equiv2+2\equiv0\pmod4$ if there is one. So a solution exists iff $4\mid p-1$, i.e. $p\equiv1\pmod4$. ∎

smt-2021-power-06.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-06.body:
For $p=2$, $a=0$ works. Let $p$ be odd. We work in the field $\mathbb F_{p^2}$ (the residues mod $p$ extended by a root of an irreducible quadratic); its nonzero elements form a cyclic group of order $p^2-1$, which is divisible by $8$. So there is an element $\zeta$ of order $8$, with $\zeta^4=-1$ (it has order $2$, and $-1$ is the only such element) and $(\zeta^2)^2=-1$, so $\zeta^{-2}=\zeta^6=-\zeta^2$. Put $\tau=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$. Then $\tau^2=\zeta^2+2+\zeta^{-2}=2$. So $a^2=2$ has exactly the two roots $\pm\tau$ in $\mathbb F_{p^2}$ ($\tau\ne-\tau$ as $p$ is odd and $\tau\neq0$). A solution exists modulo $p$ iff $\tau$ lies in $\mathbb F_p$, i.e. iff $\tau^p=\tau$ (the elements of $\mathbb F_p$ are exactly the roots of $x^p-x$). By the Frobenius identity $(u+v)^p=u^p+v^p$, $\tau^p=\zeta^p+\zeta^{-p}$, which depends on $p\bmod8$:

- $p\equiv\pm1\pmod8$: $\zeta^p=\zeta^{\pm1}$, so $\tau^p=\tau$: a solution exists.
- $p\equiv\pm3\pmod8$: $\zeta^p=\zeta^{\pm3}$ and $\zeta^3=-\zeta^{-1}$, $\zeta^{-3}=-\zeta$, so $\tau^p=-\tau\ne\tau$: no solution.

So $2$ is a square modulo an odd prime $p$ iff $p\equiv\pm1\pmod8$.

**Answer: $p=2$ or $p\equiv\pm1\pmod 8$.**

smt-2021-power-07.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-07.body:
**Setup.** A blade partition (central square $x$, blades $y\times z$) of a windmill of area $p$ is the same as a triple $(x,y,z)$ of positive integers with $x^2+4yz=p$; let $T$ be the set of these triples. A windmill can be cut into a pinwheel in two ways (reading the same shape with a different central square); algebraically the second cut of the windmill of $(x,y,z)$ is $\theta(x,y,z)$, where
$$\theta(x,y,z)=\begin{cases}(x+2z,\ z,\ y-x-z)&x<y-z,\\ (2y-x,\ y,\ x-y+z)&y-z<x<2y,\\ (x-2y,\ x-y+z,\ y)&x>2y.\end{cases}$$
So the number of blade partitions is $|T|$, the windmills are the orbits of $\theta$, and the claim is that $|T|$ is odd.

**$\theta$ is well defined.** Since $p$ is prime, $x=y-z$ is impossible ($x^2+4yz=(y+z)^2$ would be a square) and $x=2y$ is impossible ($x^2+4yz=4y(y+z)$ is divisible by $4$). So the three cases cover $T$. In each case the new triple has positive entries and the same value of $x^2+4yz$: case 1: $(x+2z)^2+4z(y-x-z)=x^2+4yz$; case 2: $(2y-x)^2+4y(x-y+z)=x^2+4yz$; case 3: $(x-2y)^2+4y(x-y+z)=x^2+4yz$.

**$\theta$ is an involution.** In case 1 the image $(x',y',z')=(x+2z,z,y-x-z)$ has $x'>2y'$ (as $x>0$), so it falls in case 3 and $\theta(x',y',z')=(x'-2y',\,x'-y'+z',\,y')=(x,y,z)$. In case 3 the image has $x'<y'-z'$ (as $z>0$), so case 1 applies and gives back $(x,y,z)$. In case 2 the image $(2y-x,y,x-y+z)$ satisfies $y'-z'<x'<2y'$, so case 2 applies again and gives $(2y-(2y-x),y,\,(2y-x)-y+(x-y+z))=(x,y,z)$.

**Exactly one fixed point.** Cases 1 and 3 change $x$ or $y$ ($z>0$, $y>0$), so they have no fixed points. In case 2, $(2y-x,y,x-y+z)=(x,y,z)$ iff $x=y$. Then $p=x^2+4xz=x(x+4z)$, so $x=1$ and $z=\frac{p-1}4$: the single fixed point $(1,1,\frac{p-1}4)$ (an integer since $p\equiv1\pmod4$; this is the one windmill with a single blade partition, the plus-shaped one). As $\theta$ is an involution, $|T|\equiv\#\text{fixed points}=1\pmod2$: the total number of blade partitions is odd. ($T$ is finite as $x,y,z\le p$.)

**Fermat.** The map $\sigma(x,y,z)=(x,z,y)$ (flipping the axes of every blade) is an involution on $T$. Since $|T|$ is odd, $\sigma$ has a fixed point, i.e. a triple with $y=z$ and $p=x^2+4y^2=x^2+(2y)^2$. ∎

smt-2021-power-08.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-08.body:
**Unit circle.** $\theta(s)=s$, a straight line from $0$ to $2\pi$, so $w=1$.

**Figure 8 (origin in the hole of the loop traversed counterclockwise).** While the point traverses the lobe around the origin counterclockwise, $\theta$ increases; while it traverses the other lobe (which does not surround the origin), the ray to the origin swings forward and then back, so $\theta$ first changes by some amount $\varepsilon$ and then returns by exactly $-\varepsilon$ (the lobe lies in a half-plane not containing the origin, so the argument stays within a range of width less than $\pi$ and returns to its starting value). The graph of $\theta$ is a continuous curve that rises overall from $0$ to $2\pi$ with one small up-and-down bump. Hence $\theta(2\pi)=2\pi$ and $w=1$ for both loops. (Equivalently, the figure 8 can be continuously deformed into the unit circle without crossing the origin, and the winding number does not change.)

**Answer: both have winding number $1$.**

smt-2021-power-09a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-09a.body: Writing $\gamma(s)=|\gamma(s)|(\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha)$ with $\alpha$ an argument of $\gamma(s)$, we have $\gamma(s)/|\gamma(s)|=e^{i\alpha}$, and $\theta(s)\equiv\alpha\pmod{2\pi}$ so $e^{i\theta(s)}=e^{i\alpha}$. ∎

smt-2021-power-09c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-09c.body: By (b), $\frac{\gamma'}{\gamma}=i\theta'+\frac{|\gamma|'}{|\gamma|}$. Integrate over $[0,2\pi]$: $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\gamma'}\gamma\,ds=i\left(\theta(2\pi)-\theta(0)\right)+\ln|\gamma|\Big|_0^{2\pi}$. The last term vanishes because $\gamma(2\pi)=\gamma(0)$, and $\theta(0)=0$, so the integral is $i\theta(2\pi)=2\pi i\,w(\gamma)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-10b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-10b.body: $h'=g'f+gf'$, so $\frac{h'}{h}=\frac{g'}{g}+\frac{f'}{f}$. Integrate and divide by $2\pi i$. ∎

smt-2021-power-11.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-11.body:
$\gamma_r'/\gamma_r=\frac{ire^{is}}{re^{is}}=i$, so $w(\gamma_r)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^{2\pi}i\,ds=1$. $f\circ\gamma_r(s)=r^{-1}e^{-is}$, whose log-derivative is $-i$, so $w(f\circ\gamma_r)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^{2\pi}(-i)\,ds=-1$.

**Answer: $1$ and $-1$.**

smt-2021-power-12a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-12a.body:
$|2|>|z|=1$ on the unit circle, so $z+2$ stays within distance $1$ of $2$: the loop is the unit circle centred at $2$, which does not enclose the origin, so $w=0$.

(Rule used: if $|g|<|h|$ on the loop, then $w(h+g)=w(h)$, because $h+g=h(1+g/h)$ and $1+g/h$ stays in the disc of radius $1$ about $1$, so it does not wind around $0$.)

**Answer: $0$**

smt-2021-power-12b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-12b.body:
On $|z|=1$, $|2z^2|=2>|z|=1$, so the loop stays within distance $1$ of $2z^2$, which winds twice around the origin ($2e^{2it}$) and never lets the loop reach the origin; hence $w=2$.

(Rule used: if $|g|<|h|$ on the loop, then $w(h+g)=w(h)$, because $h+g=h(1+g/h)$ and $1+g/h$ stays in the disc of radius $1$ about $1$, so it does not wind around $0$.)

**Answer: $2$**

smt-2021-power-12c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-12c.body:
On $|z|=1$, $\left|\frac2z\right|=2>|z^2|=1$, so the loop is a small perturbation (distance $\le1$) of $\frac2z=2e^{-it}$, which winds once clockwise; hence $w=-1$.

(Rule used: if $|g|<|h|$ on the loop, then $w(h+g)=w(h)$, because $h+g=h(1+g/h)$ and $1+g/h$ stays in the disc of radius $1$ about $1$, so it does not wind around $0$.)

**Answer: $-1$**

smt-2021-power-12d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-12d.body:
On $|z|=1$, $\left|\frac2{z^2}\right|=2>|z|=1$, so the loop is a perturbation (distance $\le1$) of $\frac2{z^2}=2e^{-2it}$, which winds twice clockwise; hence $w=-2$.

(Rule used: if $|g|<|h|$ on the loop, then $w(h+g)=w(h)$, because $h+g=h(1+g/h)$ and $1+g/h$ stays in the disc of radius $1$ about $1$, so it does not wind around $0$.)

**Answer: $-2$**

smt-2021-power-13a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-13a.body: For $|z|=1$: $|9z^8+8iz^7|=|z|^7|9z+8i|=|9z+8i|$. Also $|8iz-9|=\left|\overline{8iz-9}\right|=|-8i\bar z-9|=\left|\frac{-8i-9z}{z}\right|=|9z+8i|$, using $\bar z=1/z$. So the two moduli are equal. ∎

smt-2021-power-13b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-13b.body:
$f\circ\gamma_1=e^{7it}$ winds $7$ times. $g\circ\gamma_1=9e^{it}+8i$ is a circle of radius $9$ centred at $8i$; since $8<9$ it encloses the origin, so $w=1$ ($|8i|<|9z|$, so it winds like $9z$). $h\circ\gamma_1=8ie^{it}-9$ is a circle of radius $8$ centred at $-9$, which does not enclose the origin ($9>8$), so $w=0$.

**Answer: $7,\ 1,\ 0$.**

smt-2021-power-13c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-13c.body:
$k=\frac{fg}{h}$ since $9z^8+8iz^7=z^7(9z+8i)$. By the product and reciprocal rules, $w(k\circ\gamma_1)=w(f\circ\gamma_1)+w(g\circ\gamma_1)-w(h\circ\gamma_1)=7+1-0=8$.

**Answer: 8**

smt-2021-power-13d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-13d.body: By (a), $|k|=1$ on the unit circle, so $k\circ\gamma_1$ is a loop on the unit circle with winding number $8$: its argument increases by a net $16\pi$ over $[0,2\pi]$, so it passes through the angle $\pi$ (mod $2\pi$) at least $8$ times, at distinct parameter values $s_1,\dots,s_8\in[0,2\pi)$. At those points $k=-1$, i.e. $9z^8+8iz^7=-(8iz-9)$, i.e. $9z^8+8iz^7+8iz-9=0$ at the $8$ distinct points $z=e^{is_j}$. A polynomial of degree $8$ has at most $8$ roots, so these are all its roots, all on $|z|=1$. ∎

smt-2021-power-14a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-14a.body:
$f(z)=1+\frac4z+\frac{17}{z^2}+\frac{2021}{z^3}$. For $|z|=r$ large, $\left|\frac4z+\frac{17}{z^2}+\frac{2021}{z^3}\right|\le\frac4r+\frac{17}{r^2}+\frac{2021}{r^3}<1$, so $\operatorname{Re}f>0$: the loop $f\circ\gamma_r$ stays in the right half-plane, near $1$, and does not wind around the origin: $w=0$. Then $p\circ\gamma_r=\gamma_r^3\cdot(f\circ\gamma_r)$ and $w(\gamma_r^3)=3$, so $w(p\circ\gamma_r)=3+0=3$.

**Answer: $0$ and $3$.**

smt-2021-power-14b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-14b.body:
$\gamma_0(t)=0$ for all $t$, so $p\circ\gamma_0$ is the constant loop at $p(0)=2021\ne0$; a constant loop does not wind around the origin, so $w=0$. (This differs from $w(p\circ\gamma_r)=3$ for large $r$, which gives the contradiction: deforming $r$ from large to $0$ keeps $p\circ\gamma_r$ in $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ if $p$ has no roots, so the winding number would be constant.)

**Answer: 0**

smt-2021-power-14c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-14c.body: The winding number is defined for loops that avoid the origin. If $p$ had a root $z_0$, then for $r=|z_0|$ the loop $p\circ\gamma_r$ would pass through $0$, so $w(p\circ\gamma_r)$ would not be defined and the deformation from large $r$ to $r=0$ would not stay inside $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$: the winding number could change when $r$ crosses $|z_0|$.

smt-2021-power-15.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-15.body: Let $f(z)=-z$. It is continuous and $|f(z)|=|z|$, so it maps $D\setminus\{0\}$ into itself, and $f(z)=z$ would give $2z=0$, i.e. $z=0$, which is excluded. So $f$ has no fixed point. ∎

smt-2021-power-16a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-16a.body:
On $|z|=1$ we have $g(z)=z$, so $g\circ\gamma_1=\gamma_1$, which winds once around the origin: $w=1$.

**Answer: 1**

smt-2021-power-16b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-16b.body:
$\gamma_0$ is the constant loop at $0$, so $g\circ\gamma_0$ is constant (a single point on the unit circle), which has winding number $0$.

**Answer: 0**

smt-2021-power-16c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-16c.body:
$|g|^2=1$ gives $|f+\lambda(z-f)|^2=1$. With $A=|z-f|^2=(a-c)^2+(b-d)^2>0$ (as $f(z)\ne z$), $B=f\cdot(z-f)=c(a-c)+d(b-d)$ and $C=|f|^2-1=c^2+d^2-1\le0$: $A\lambda^2+2B\lambda+C=0$. Its roots are $\lambda=\frac{-B\pm\sqrt{B^2-AC}}{A}$; since $AC\le0$ we have $B^2-AC\ge B^2\ge0$, so the square root is real, and $\sqrt{B^2-AC}\ge|B|$, so the root with $+$ is $\ge0$ (the other is $\le0$). The ray from $f(z)$ through $z$ corresponds to $\lambda\ge0$ (with $\lambda=1$ at $z$ itself when $|z|=1$), so $\lambda=\frac{-B+\sqrt{B^2-AC}}{A}$.

This expression is a continuous function of $(a,b,c,d)$ as long as $A>0$, which holds since $f(z)\neq z$. Since $f$ is continuous in $z$, $\lambda$ and hence $g(z)=f(z)+\lambda(z-f(z))$ are continuous in $z$. ∎

smt-2021-power-16d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-16d.body: The ray from $f(z)$ through $z$ (and hence $g(z)$) is only defined if $f(z)\ne z$ (otherwise there is no direction). It was also needed for $A>0$ in part (c), so that $g$ is continuous. Without the assumption we cannot construct $g$, which is exactly what produces the contradiction $w(g\circ\gamma_1)=1\ne0=w(g\circ\gamma_0)$ by continuous deformation of $\gamma_r$ from $r=1$ to $r=0$.

smt-2021-power-17.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-17.body:
The vertices $A,B,C$ are coloured $r,g,y$ respectively ($A$ is on $AB$ and $AC$, so it has colour $r$ (the only common colour), etc.).

Call an edge of $T$ an *$rg$-edge* if its endpoints have colours $r$ and $g$. Count pairs (triangle, $rg$-edge of that triangle). A triangle with vertex colours $\{r,g,y\}$ has exactly one $rg$-edge; a triangle coloured with only $r$ and $g$ (two vertices of one colour, one of the other) has exactly two $rg$-edges; other triangles have none. So the number $N$ of pairs is congruent mod $2$ to the number of triangles with all three colours.

On the other hand each $rg$-edge in the interior belongs to two triangles, and each $rg$-edge on the boundary of $ABC$ belongs to one triangle. A boundary edge can be an $rg$-edge only on side $AB$ (sides $AC$ and $BC$ have no vertex coloured both $r$ and $g$... side $AC$ uses $r,y$, $BC$ uses $g,y$). So $N\equiv$ (number of $rg$-edges on $AB$) mod $2$. Going from $A$ (colour $r$) to $B$ (colour $g$) along the vertices on $AB$, each of coloured $r$ or $g$, the colour changes an odd number of times, so the number of $rg$-edges on $AB$ is odd.

Hence the number of three-coloured triangles is odd, in particular at least one. ∎

smt-2021-power-18a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-18a.body:
$\varphi(5)=4$ (all of $1,\dots,4$). $15=3\cdot5$: the numbers up to $15$ coprime to $15$ are $1,2,4,7,8,11,13,14$: $8$. $45=3^2\cdot5$: remove the multiples of $3$ ($15$) and of $5$ ($9$), add back the multiples of $15$ ($3$): $45-15-9+3=24$.

**Answer: $4,\ 8,\ 24$.**

smt-2021-power-18b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-18b.body: For a prime power, the numbers in $1..p^k$ not coprime to $p^k$ are the multiples of $p$, of which there are $p^{k-1}$; so $\varphi(p^k)=p^k-p^{k-1}=p^{k-1}(p-1)$. If $\gcd(m,n)=1$ then $\varphi(mn)=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)$: by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, residues $r$ mod $mn$ correspond bijectively to pairs $(r\bmod m,r\bmod n)$, and $r$ is coprime to $mn$ iff it is coprime to both $m$ and $n$. Applying this to the prime powers gives $\varphi(n)=\prod p_i^{k_i-1}(p_i-1)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-19a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-19a.body: A fraction $\frac kn$ reduces to $\frac ab$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$, $b\mid n$, and $1\le a\le b$. Conversely each such $\frac ab$ with $b\mid n$ occurs exactly once (as $\frac{a\,n/b}{n}$). The number of reduced fractions with denominator $d$ is the number of $a\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ coprime to $d$, which is $\varphi(d)$. Every divisor $d$ of $n$ occurs, and no other denominators.

smt-2021-power-19b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-19b.body: The $n$ fractions $\frac1n,\dots,\frac nn$ are sorted by their denominator $d$ when reduced; by part (a) there are $\varphi(d)$ with denominator $d$, for each $d\mid n$. So $n=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-20.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-20.body: Let $r_1,\dots,r_{\varphi(n)}$ be the residues mod $n$ that are coprime to $n$. Since $\gcd(a,n)=1$, the numbers $ar_i$ are also coprime to $n$ and pairwise incongruent (if $ar_i\equiv ar_j$ then $n\mid a(r_i-r_j)$, so $n\mid r_i-r_j$). Hence $ar_1,\dots,ar_{\varphi(n)}$ is a permutation of $r_1,\dots,r_{\varphi(n)}$ modulo $n$. Comparing products: $a^{\varphi(n)}\prod r_i\equiv\prod r_i$, and $\prod r_i$ is coprime to $n$, so we may cancel it. ∎

smt-2021-power-21a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-21a.body: For $a>b$: $x^a-1=x^{a-b}(x^b-1)+(x^{a-b}-1)$, so $\gcd(x^a-1,x^b-1)=\gcd(x^{a-b}-1,x^b-1)$. Repeating (the subtractive Euclidean algorithm on the exponents) we reach $\gcd(x^g-1,x^g-1)=x^g-1$ with $g=\gcd(a,b)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-22a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-22a.body: Send $\frac kn$ to $e^{2\pi ik/n}$. This is a bijection onto the $n$-th roots of unity. If $\frac kn$ reduces to $\frac ab$ then $e^{2\pi ik/n}=e^{2\pi ia/b}$, which has order exactly $b$ since $\gcd(a,b)=1$: it is a primitive $b$-th root of unity.

smt-2021-power-22b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-22b.body: $x^n-1=\prod_{\zeta^n=1}(x-\zeta)$ (it has $n$ distinct roots). By part (a), the $n$-th roots of unity are partitioned according to their order $d$, which divides $n$, and for each $d\mid n$ the roots of order $d$ are exactly the primitive $d$-th roots, whose product $\prod(x-\zeta)$ is $\Phi_d(x)$. Hence $x^n-1=\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(x)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-23.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-23.body: Two monic integer polynomials are coprime iff they have no common complex root: a common root $\zeta$ has a monic integer minimal polynomial (Gauss's lemma) dividing both, and a common non-constant divisor has a common root. The roots of $x^n-1$ are the $n$-th roots of unity, all simple. A divisor of $x^n-1$ that is coprime to every $x^k-1$ ($k<n$) can therefore have only roots $\zeta$ with $\zeta^k\ne1$ for all $k<n$, i.e. primitive $n$-th roots of unity, and each at most once; so its degree is at most $\varphi(n)$. $\Phi_n$ is a divisor of $x^n-1$ whose roots are exactly the primitive $n$-th roots, hence is coprime to each $x^k-1$ ($k<n$) and has the largest possible degree. ∎

smt-2021-power-24b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-24b.body: The divisors of $p$ are $1,p$, so $\Phi_p=\frac{x^p-1}{x-1}=x^{p-1}+\cdots+1$. The divisors of $p^k$ are $1,p,\dots,p^k$, so $\Phi_{p^k}=\frac{x^{p^k}-1}{x^{p^{k-1}}-1}=1+x^{p^{k-1}}+\cdots+x^{(p-1)p^{k-1}}=\Phi_p(x^{p^{k-1}})$.

smt-2021-power-24c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-24c.body: For odd $n$, $\zeta$ is a primitive $n$-th root of unity iff $-\zeta$ is a primitive $2n$-th root of unity ($-\zeta$ has order $\operatorname{lcm}(2,n)=2n$). So $\Phi_{2n}(x)=\pm\Phi_n(-x)$, and comparing leading coefficients gives $\Phi_{2p}(x)=\Phi_p(-x)$ ($\deg=p-1$ is even, so the sign is $+$). For $k\ge2$, the primitive $2^kp$-th roots of unity are the $\omega$ with $\omega^{2^{k-1}}$ a primitive $2p$-th root, so $\Phi_{2^kp}(x)=\Phi_{2p}(x^{2^{k-1}})=\Phi_p(-x^{2^{k-1}})$; this is also correct for $k=1$.

smt-2021-power-24d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-24d.body: The roots of $\Phi_m(x^{p^k})$ are the $\omega$ with $\omega^{p^k}$ a primitive $m$-th root of unity; since $p\nmid m$ their orders are $m\cdot p^j$ with $0\le j\le k$, and the roots of order $mp^j$ are those of $\Phi_{mp^j}$. So $\Phi_m(x^{p^k})=\prod_{j=0}^{k}\Phi_{mp^j}(x)$, and dividing by the same identity with $k-1$ gives the formula.

smt-2021-power-25.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-25.body: By strong induction on $n$. $\Phi_1=x-1$. For $n\ge2$, $\Phi_n=\frac{x^n-1}{G}$ with $G=\prod_{d\mid n,d<n}\Phi_d$, which is a monic integer polynomial by induction. Long division of $x^n-1$ by the monic integer polynomial $G$ produces a quotient with integer coefficients (each step subtracts an integer multiple of $G$, since the leading coefficient of $G$ is $1$) and the remainder is $0$ (because $G\mid x^n-1$ over $\mathbb C$, and the remainder is unique). So $\Phi_n$ is a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. ∎

smt-2021-power-26b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-26b.body: The roots of $\Phi_n(x^k)$ are the $\omega$ with $\omega^k$ a primitive $n$-th root of unity. If $\omega$ has order $m$ then $\omega^k$ has order $\frac m{\gcd(m,k)}$, so we need $\frac m{\gcd(m,k)}=n$. Put $g=\gcd(m,k)$, so $m=ng$ with $g\mid k$ and $\gcd(ng,k)=g$, i.e. $\gcd(n,k/g)=1$. Conversely each such $g$ gives $m=ng$ with $\frac{m}{\gcd(m,k)}=n$. Since $\Phi_n(x^k)$ has simple roots (it divides $x^{nk}-1$) and the roots of order $m$ form $\Phi_m$: $\Phi_n(x^k)=\prod_{g\mid k,\ \gcd(n,k/g)=1}\Phi_{ng}(x)$. In particular, if $\gcd(n,k)=1$ this is $\prod_{g\mid k}\Phi_{ng}(x)$, and if every prime factor of $k$ divides $n$ it is just $\Phi_{nk}(x)$.

smt-2021-power-27.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-27.body:
From $x^n-1=\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(x)$ and $\Phi_1=x-1$: $\frac{x^n-1}{x-1}=\prod_{d\mid n,d>1}\Phi_d(x)$, and the left side equals $n$ at $x=1$. So $n=\prod_{d\mid n,\,d>1}\Phi_d(1)$ $(*)$.

We induct on $n$. If $n=p^k$: the divisors $d>1$ are $p,\dots,p^k$, and by induction $\Phi_{p^j}(1)=p$ for $j<k$, so $(*)$ gives $\Phi_{p^k}(1)=\frac{p^k}{p^{k-1}}=p$. If $n=\prod p_i^{a_i}$ has at least two prime factors: by induction, among the divisors $d$ with $1<d<n$, $\Phi_d(1)=p_i$ if $d=p_i^j$ ($1\le j\le a_i$) and $1$ otherwise, so $\prod_{1<d<n}\Phi_d(1)=\prod p_i^{a_i}=n$. Then $(*)$ gives $n=n\cdot\Phi_n(1)$, so $\Phi_n(1)=1$. ∎

smt-2021-power-28.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-28.body:
**Bound.** If a prime $q$ divides $2^n-1=\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d(2)$, then $q\mid\Phi_d(2)$ for some $d\mid n$ and $q\le\Phi_d(2)=\prod|2-\zeta|\le3^{\varphi(d)}\le3^{\varphi(n)}$ (each primitive $d$-th root $\zeta$ has $|2-\zeta|\le3$, and $\varphi(d)\le\varphi(n)$ for $d\mid n$). So every prime factor of $2^n-1$ is at most $3^{\varphi(n)}=2^{\varphi(n)\log_23}$, and it suffices that $\varphi(n)\log_23\le\frac n{2021}$, i.e. $\frac{\varphi(n)}n\le\frac1{2021\log_23}\ (\approx\frac1{3203})$.

**Many such $n$.** $\frac{\varphi(n)}n=\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right)\le\exp\left(-\sum_{p\mid n}\frac1p\right)$. Since $\sum_p\frac1p$ diverges, there is $N_0=p_1p_2\cdots p_r$ (a product of the first $r$ primes) with $\sum_{i\le r}\frac1{p_i}>\ln3203$, so $\frac{\varphi(N_0)}{N_0}<\frac1{3203}$. Every multiple $n=mN_0$ has $\frac{\varphi(n)}n\le\frac{\varphi(N_0)}{N_0}$ (it has the same prime factors or more), and there are infinitely many such $n$. ∎

smt-2021-power-29.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-29.body:
Suppose $x^5-x-1=f\,g$ with non-constant integer polynomials (monic after sign changes; constant terms multiply to $-1$).

*Linear factor.* It would be $x\pm1$, but $1^5-1-1=-1$ and $(-1)^5+1-1=-1$ are nonzero.

*Quadratic times cubic.* Write $(x^2+ax+b)(x^3+cx^2+dx+e)$ with $be=-1$. Expanding gives the equations $a+c=0$, $b+ac+d=0$, $e+ad+bc=0$, $ae+bd=-1$, $be=-1$.

- $b=1,e=-1$: $c=-a$, $d=a^2-1$, and $e+ad+bc=-1+a(a^2-1)-a=a^3-2a-1=(a+1)(a^2-a-1)=0$ forces (integer) $a=-1$, hence $d=0$ and $ae+bd=1\ne-1$: contradiction.
- $b=-1,e=1$: $c=-a$, $d=a^2+1$, and $e+ad+bc=1+a(a^2+1)+a=a^3+2a+1=0$ has no integer root ($a=\pm1$ give $4,-2$): contradiction.

So no factorisation exists. ∎

smt-2021-power-30a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-30a.body: $\binom pk$ is divisible by $p$ for $0<k<p$, so $(x-1)^p=x^p+(-1)^p\equiv x^p-1\pmod p$ (for $p=2$, $(-1)^2=1\equiv-1$). Thus $(x-1)\Phi_p(x)=x^p-1\equiv(x-1)^p$, and dividing by $x-1$ (the ring of polynomials over $\mathbb F_p$ has no zero-divisors) gives $\Phi_p(x)\equiv(x-1)^{p-1}$. ∎

smt-2021-power-30b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-30b.body: Over $\mathbb F_p$, $y^{p-1}$ factors uniquely into irreducibles $y$, so $f\equiv y^s$ and $g\equiv y^t$ with $s,t\ge1$. Hence the constant terms $f(0),g(0)$ are divisible by $p$, and $f(0)g(0)$ is divisible by $p^2$. ∎

smt-2021-power-30c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-30c.body: Put $x=y+1$: $\Phi_p(y+1)\equiv y^{p-1}\pmod p$ by (a), and its constant term is $\Phi_p(1)=p$, not divisible by $p^2$. If $\Phi_p=FG$ with non-constant integer polynomials (monic), then $\Phi_p(y+1)=F(y+1)G(y+1)\equiv y^{p-1}$, contradicting (b). So $\Phi_p$ is irreducible. ∎

smt-2021-power-31a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-31a.body: Let $\zeta$ be a root of $\Phi_n$, i.e. a primitive $n$-th root of unity. As $\gcd(k,n)=1$, $\zeta^k$ is also a primitive $n$-th root of unity, so $\Phi_n(\zeta^k)=0$: $\zeta$ is a root of $\Phi_n(x^k)$. The roots of $\Phi_n$ are simple, so $\Phi_n(x)\mid\Phi_n(x^k)$ over $\mathbb C$, and, $\Phi_n$ being monic with integer coefficients, also over $\mathbb Z$ (long division by a monic integer polynomial stays in $\mathbb Z[x]$). ∎

smt-2021-power-31b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-31b.body: Modulo $p$ we have $(u+v)^p\equiv u^p+v^p$ for polynomials $u,v$ (the binomial coefficients $\binom pj$, $0<j<p$, are divisible by $p$), so for $f=\sum c_jx^j$: $f(x)^p\equiv\sum c_j^px^{jp}\equiv\sum c_jx^{jp}=f(x^p)$, using Fermat's little theorem $c_j^p\equiv c_j$. ∎

smt-2021-power-31c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-31c.body: Since $f\mid x^n-1$ and $n\mid p-k$, $x^n-1$ divides $x^{p-k}-1$ and hence $x^p-x^k=x^k(x^{p-k}-1)$; so $f\mid x^p-x^k$. For any polynomial $f$, $u-v$ divides $f(u)-f(v)$; with $u=x^p$, $v=x^k$ we get $x^p-x^k\mid f(x^p)-f(x^k)$, so $f(x^p)\equiv f(x^k)\pmod f$. Also $f(x)^p\equiv0\pmod f$. Hence $f(x^p)-f(x)^p\equiv f(x^k)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-31d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-31d.body: Write $p\,g=q\,f+h$ with $q$ an integer polynomial. Reduce modulo $p$: $0\equiv\bar q\bar f+\bar h$ in $\mathbb F_p[x]$. Since $f$ is monic, $\bar f$ has the same degree as $f$ and is monic. If $\bar q\ne0$ then $\deg(\bar q\bar f)\ge\deg f>\deg h\ge\deg\bar h$, so $\bar q\bar f+\bar h\ne0$: contradiction. So $\bar q=0$ and hence $\bar h=0$: $p$ divides all coefficients of $h$. ∎

smt-2021-power-31e.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-31e.body:
Let $r$ be the remainder of $h$ on division by the monic $f$ ($\deg r<\deg f$). Then $r\equiv h\equiv p\,g\pmod f$, so by (d) all coefficients of $r$ are divisible by $p$. If this holds for infinitely many primes, each coefficient of $r$ is zero, so $r=0$ and $f\mid h$.

Now let $p\nmid n$ be a large prime and $k=p\bmod n$. By (b), $f(x^p)-f(x)^p=p\,G(x)$ for an integer polynomial $G$, and by (c) this is $\equiv f(x^k)\pmod f$; hence $f(x^k)\equiv p\,G\pmod f$. Let $r_k$ be the remainder of $f(x^k)$ on division by $f$; by (d) $p$ divides all coefficients of $r_k$. There are only finitely many residues $k$ (with $0\le k<n$), hence finitely many polynomials $r_k$; if $p$ exceeds the absolute value of every nonzero coefficient of every $r_k$, then $r_k=0$, so $f\mid f(x^k)$. Since $f(x^p)\equiv f(x^k)\pmod f$ (by (c)), $f(x)\mid f(x^p)$ for all large primes $p$. ∎

smt-2021-power-31f.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-31f.body:
Let $N=n\cdot\prod_{q\le C,\ q
mid k}q+k$ (product over primes). Then $N\equiv k\pmod n$. Let $q\le C$ be prime. If $q
mid k$, then $q$ divides the product term, so $N\equiv k
ot\equiv0\pmod q$. If $q\mid k$ then $q
mid n$ (as $\gcd(k,n)=1$) and $q$ does not divide the product, so $N\equiv n\prod
ot\equiv0\pmod q$. So $N$ has no prime factor $\le C$.

Write $N=q_1q_2\cdots q_s$ (primes $>C$). Since $f(x)\mid f(x^{q_1})$, substituting $x	o x^{q_1}$ gives $f(x^{q_1})\mid f(x^{q_1q_2})$, and so on: $f(x)\mid f(x^{q_1})\mid f(x^{q_1q_2})\mid\cdots\mid f(x^N)$. As $f\mid x^n-1\mid x^{N-k}-1$, $f\mid x^N-x^k$, so $f\mid f(x^N)-f(x^k)$. Together $f(x)\mid f(x^k)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-32a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-32a.body: $\zeta$ is a root of the integer polynomial $P-Q$. Since $\Phi_n$ is the (monic) minimal polynomial of $\zeta$ (it is irreducible), $\Phi_n\mid P-Q$. For $\gcd(k,n)=1$, $\zeta^k$ is a root of $\Phi_n$, hence of $P-Q$. ∎

smt-2021-power-32b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-32b.body: Suppose $S=\zeta^{a_1}+\cdots+\zeta^{a_k}=m$ is a nonzero integer, where $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}$ and each $\gcd(a_i,n)=1$. Let $P(x)=x^{a_1}+\cdots+x^{a_k}$ and $Q(x)=m$. By (a), $P(\zeta^j)=m$ for all $j$ coprime to $n$. Summing over the $\varphi(n)$ such $j$ (with $\zeta^j$ running over all primitive $n$-th roots): $\varphi(n)\,m=\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{j}\zeta^{ja_i}=k\,\mu(n)$, because for each $i$ the numbers $\zeta^{ja_i}$ run over all primitive $n$-th roots of unity as $j$ does, whose sum is $\mu(n)$ (Problem 34c). Since $m\ne0$ we get $\varphi(n)\le\varphi(n)|m|=k|\mu(n)|\le k$. But $\varphi(n)\to\infty$ ($\varphi(n)\ge\sqrt{n/2}$), so only finitely many $n$ satisfy $\varphi(n)\le k$. ∎

smt-2021-power-33b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-33b.body: $F(m)=f(m)+\sum_{d\mid m,d<m}f(d)$, so $f(m)=F(m)-\sum_{d\mid m,d<m}f(d)$: by induction on $m$, each $f(m)$ is an integer linear combination of the $F(d)$, $d\mid m$.

smt-2021-power-33c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-33c.body: By the recursion $f(m)=F(m)-\sum_{d\mid m,d<m}f(d)$, the expression of $f(m)$ in terms of the $F(e)$ involves only $e\mid m$ and its coefficients are determined by $m$ alone (the unique solution of a triangular system). So $c_{n,d,m}=c_{d,m}$.

smt-2021-power-33d.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-33d.body: Fix $d$ and define $f_d(x)=f(x/d)$ if $d\mid x$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $F_d(m):=\sum_{e\mid m}f_d(e)=F(m/d)$ if $d\mid m$ (and $0$ otherwise). Applying the inversion formula to the pair $(f_d,F_d)$ at a multiple $m$ of $d$: $f(m/d)=f_d(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}c_{e,m}F_d(e)=\sum_{u\mid m/d}c_{du,m}F(u)$, while directly $f(m/d)=\sum_{u\mid m/d}c_{u,m/d}F(u)$. Since $F$ is arbitrary, $c_{du,m}=c_{u,m/d}$; with $u=1$, $c_{d,m}=c_{1,m/d}$, which depends only on $m/d$. Define $\mu(k)=c_{1,k}$, so $f(m)=\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(m/d)F(d)$. Taking $f=\delta_1$ ($f(1)=1$, else $0$, so $F\equiv1$) gives $\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d)=[m=1]$, which determines $\mu$ recursively. Computing: $\mu(1)=1$, $\mu(p)=-1$, $\mu(p^k)=0$ for $k\ge2$ (the sum over $d\mid p^k$ telescopes), and $\mu$ is multiplicative ($\mu(ab)=\mu(a)\mu(b)$ for coprime $a,b$, by induction using $\sum_{d\mid ab}\mu(d)=\sum_{d_1\mid a}\mu(d_1)\sum_{d_2\mid b}\mu(d_2)$). Hence $\mu(n)=(-1)^r$ if $n$ is a product of $r$ distinct primes and $\mu(n)=0$ if $n$ has a repeated prime factor (the Möbius function). So $f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)F(d)$ (Möbius inversion).

smt-2021-power-34a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-34a.body: From $\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n$ (Problem 19b) and Möbius inversion: $\varphi(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\frac nd=n\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{\mu(d)}d$. Only squarefree $d$ contribute: $\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{\mu(d)}{d}=\sum_{S\subseteq\{p\mid n\}}\prod_{p\in S}\left(-\frac1p\right)=\prod_{p\mid n}\left(1-\frac1p\right)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-34b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-34b.body: Since $x^m-1=\prod_{e\mid m}\Phi_e(x)$: $\prod_{d\mid n}(x^d-1)^{\mu(n/d)}=\prod_{d\mid n}\prod_{e\mid d}\Phi_e^{\mu(n/d)}=\prod_{e\mid n}\Phi_e^{\sum_{e\mid d\mid n}\mu(n/d)}$. The exponent is $\sum_{t\mid n/e}\mu(t)=[n=e]$, so the product is $\Phi_n(x)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-34c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-34c.body: Let $s_d$ be the sum of the primitive $d$-th roots of unity. Every $n$-th root of unity is a primitive $d$-th root of unity for exactly one $d\mid n$, so $\sum_{d\mid n}s_d$ is the sum of all $n$-th roots of unity, which is $0$ for $n>1$ and $1$ for $n=1$ (it is minus the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ in $x^n-1$). That is $[n=1]$. By Möbius inversion, $s_n=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)[d=1]=\mu(n)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-35a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-35a.body: By Problem 34b, $\Phi_{pq}=\frac{(x^{pq}-1)(x-1)}{(x^p-1)(x^q-1)}$. Since $\deg\Phi_{pq}=(p-1)(q-1)<pq$, $\Phi_{pq}$ is determined by its power series modulo $x^{pq}$, and modulo $x^{pq}$ we have $\Phi_{pq}\equiv\frac{(1-x)}{(1-x^p)(1-x^q)}$ (the factors $x^{pq}-1\equiv-1$ and $(x-1)/((x^p-1)(x^q-1))=-(1-x)/((1-x^p)(1-x^q))$ combine to this). Now $\frac1{(1-x^p)(1-x^q)}=\sum_{m\ge0}c_mx^m$ where $c_m$ is the number of pairs $(a,b)$ of non-negative integers with $ap+bq=m$. For $m<pq$ there is at most one such pair: if $ap+bq=a'p+b'q$ then $p\mid(b-b')q$ so $p\mid b-b'$, and $|b-b'|<p$ (as $bq\le m<pq$) forces $b=b'$ and then $a=a'$. So $c_m\in\{0,1\}$ for $m<pq$, and the coefficient of $x^m$ in $\Phi_{pq}$ is $c_m-c_{m-1}\in\{-1,0,1\}$ (with $c_{-1}=0$). ∎

smt-2021-power-35b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-35b.body: Take primes $p<q<r<2p$ (e.g. $7,11,13$) and $n=pqr$. By Problem 34b, $\Phi_n=\frac{(x^{pqr}-1)(x^p-1)(x^q-1)(x^r-1)}{(x^{pq}-1)(x^{pr}-1)(x^{qr}-1)(x-1)}$. Modulo $x^{pq}$ (note $pq>2p>r$ and $pq>p+q$) the four factors $x^{pqr}-1,\ x^{pq}-1,\ x^{pr}-1,\ x^{qr}-1$ are all $\equiv-1$, so the one in the numerator cancels against one of the three in the denominator up to the sign $(-1)/(-1)^3=1$, and $\Phi_n\equiv\frac{(x^p-1)(x^q-1)(x^r-1)}{x-1}=\frac{(1-x^p)(1-x^q)(1-x^r)}{1-x}\pmod{x^{pq}}$ (three sign changes in the numerator and one in the denominator give an overall $+$). Modulo $x^{p+q}$ (and $r<p+q$): $(1-x^p)(1-x^q)(1-x^r)\equiv1-x^p-x^q-x^r$, and dividing by $1-x$ means multiplying by $1+x+x^2+\cdots$, so the coefficient of $x^m$ is $1-[m\ge p]-[m\ge q]-[m\ge r]$ for $m<p+q$. At $m=r$ this is $1-1-1-1=-2$ (as $p<q<r$). Since $\deg\Phi_n=(p-1)(q-1)(r-1)>r$ the coefficient is really a coefficient of $\Phi_n$. So $\Phi_{1001}$ has a coefficient $-2$ at $x^{13}$: not flat. ∎

smt-2021-power-36a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-36a.body: $x^2\equiv-1$ so $p\nmid x$, and $1\equiv x^{p-1}=(x^2)^{(p-1)/2}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p$. smt-2021-power-37a.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-37a.body: If $q$ is a prime factor of $a^n-1$ not dividing $a^m-1$ for $m<n$, then $\operatorname{ord}_q(a)=n$ (the order divides $n$ and no smaller $m$ works), so $n\mid q-1$ by Fermat. Suppose only finitely many primes $\equiv1\pmod n$, say the set $S$. Take $a=2021\prod_{p\in S}p\ (\ge2021)$. The theorem gives a prime $q\equiv1\pmod n$ dividing $a^n-1$, hence $q\nmid a$, so $q\notin S$: contradiction. ∎

smt-2021-power-37b.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-37b.body: $2^{2^n}-1=(2^{2^{n-1}}-1)(2^{2^{n-1}}+1)$. Let $q$ be a prime factor of $2^{2^{n-1}}+1$ (it is $\ge3$, so such a prime exists). The numbers $2^{2^{n-1}}+1$ and $2^{2^{n-1}}-1$ are odd and differ by $2$, so they are coprime; hence $q\nmid2^{2^{n-1}}-1$. For $m<n$, $2^{2^m}-1$ divides $2^{2^{n-1}}-1$ (as $2^m\mid2^{n-1}$), so $q\nmid2^{2^m}-1$. ∎

smt-2021-power-37c.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-37c.body: Let $e=m/d$. If $\zeta$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity, then $\zeta^d$ has order $m/\gcd(m,d)=e$, so $\Phi_e(\zeta^d)=0$; hence $\Phi_m(x)\mid\Phi_e(x^d)$ (roots of $\Phi_m$ are simple; division stays in $\mathbb Z[x]$ as $\Phi_m$ is monic). So $\Phi_m(a)\mid\Phi_e(a^d)$. Also $a^d-1\mid\Phi_e(a^d)-\Phi_e(1)$ (since $u-1\mid g(u)-g(1)$ for any integer polynomial $g$). Let $G=\gcd(\Phi_m(a),a^d-1)$. Then $G\mid\Phi_e(a^d)$ and $G\mid\Phi_e(a^d)-\Phi_e(1)$, so $G\mid\Phi_e(1)=\Phi_{m/d}(1)$. ∎

smt-2021-power-37e.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-37e.body:
Let $a\ge2021$, $n\ge3$. It suffices to find a prime $q\mid\Phi_n(a)$ that does not divide $a^m-1$ for any $m<n$: then $q\mid a^n-1$ and $\operatorname{ord}_q(a)=n$.

Suppose not: every prime $q\mid\Phi_n(a)$ has $d=\operatorname{ord}_q(a)<n$. By Problem 37d, for each such $q$: $n=dq^j$ with $j\ge1$ (so $q\mid n$) and $q^2\nmid\Phi_n(a)$ (as $n\ne2$). Hence $\Phi_n(a)$ is a squarefree product of primes dividing $n$, so $\Phi_n(a)\le\prod_{q\mid n}q\le n$.

On the other hand $\Phi_n(a)=\prod|a-\zeta|\ge(a-1)^{\varphi(n)}\ge2020^{\varphi(n)}$ (the product is over the primitive $n$-th roots $\zeta$, and $|a-\zeta|\ge a-1$). For $n\ge3$, $\varphi(n)\ge2$, so $\Phi_n(a)\ge2020^2=4{,}080{,}400$, which exceeds $n$ when $n<4{,}080{,}400$. For larger $n$ use $\varphi(n)\ge\sqrt{n/2}$ (indeed $\varphi(p^k)\ge p^{k/2}$ for odd $p$ and $\varphi(2^k)=2^{k-1}\ge\sqrt{2^k/2}$, and $\varphi$ is multiplicative), so $\Phi_n(a)\ge2020^{\sqrt{n/2}}>n$ for $n\ge4{,}080{,}400$ (already $2020^{1421}\gg2\cdot1421^2$ and the left side grows much faster). Contradiction in all cases. ∎

smt-2021-power-37f.title: Solution
smt-2021-power-37f.body:
*The infinite family.* $n=2$, $a=2^k-1$ for $k\ge2$: $a^2-1=(a-1)(a+1)=(2^k-2)2^k=2^{k+1}(2^{k-1}-1)$. The prime factor $2$ divides $a-1$, and every prime factor of $2^{k-1}-1$ divides $2^k-2=a-1$ (as $2^{k-1}-1\mid2(2^{k-1}-1)=a-1$). So every prime factor of $a^2-1$ already divides $a^1-1$.

*The single case.* $(a,n)=(2,6)$: $2^6-1=63=3^2\cdot7$, with $3\mid2^2-1=3$ and $7\mid2^3-1=7$, so both primes already divide $2^m-1$ for $m=2,3<6$.
